# CSCI 435 PR review

You are drafting a code review that the user (GitHub login `ab-wm`) will test, edit and post on a
teammate's PR in `CSCI-435-SE/gitea`, a course fork of Gitea. The review is a graded course
deliverable, so the user stays its author: you gather the facts, check them, and hand back a
draft in their format. Don't post, approve or comment on the PR, and don't push to it. Don't offer
to fix the author's code either. In this course the author makes each change themselves, one
change per commit.

The user's standing instruction for reviews is "not *that* deep". That doesn't mean overlooking
real problems, and it doesn't mean nitpicking every small one. The code is not going upstream. A
finding belongs in the draft only if it would change a score, or if the author would want to know
about it before merging.

## 1. Find your footing

Work out where you are running, because that decides how you fetch the PR and where the draft goes.

- **Claude Code inside the repo clone** (`gh` works, and the working tree is the fork). Use `gh`
  for PR data and read source files locally. The user is usually on their own feature branch, so
  don't switch it. Fetch the PR head with `git fetch origin pull/<N>/head:pr-<N>` and read files
  with `git show pr-<N>:<path>`. Compare with `git diff origin/main...pr-<N>`, because local
  `main` is often behind.
- **Chat, or anywhere without the clone.** The repo is public. Use a GitHub connector if one is
  attached. Otherwise fetch the URLs in `references/fetching-without-the-repo.md`. If nothing can
  reach GitHub, ask the user for the PR link and the diff.

## 2. Triage

First get the PR's title, author, changed files and linked issue (`Closes #N`). Then decide how
much review it needs. The user only does a full review when code changed:

- **The PR is already merged, or the user has already reviewed it.** Say so first, quoting their
  existing review in a line. Continue only if they want a fresh look, for example a re-review
  after new commits. Don't let their earlier scores steer yours.
- **The user approved, and commits were pushed after that.** In Sprint 3 a PR may only be merged
  after an approval on its latest commit, so it needs a new approval. Check only the new commits,
  as in a follow-up, and suggest a short re-approval if they're fine.
- **The PR only touches check-ins, docs, course files, showcase material, AI logs, or config like
  `.coderabbit.yaml`.** Skip the rubric. Skim the files for anything surprising, such as code
  hiding in a "docs" PR, a secret, or a file in the wrong folder. Then suggest a one-line
  approval in the user's voice, for example "All good, just the check-in doc and AI log. No need
  for complete review."
- **The PR is a mutation-testing write-up** (`docs/sprint3/mutation/**`). If it holds only the
  write-up and the reports, treat it like a docs PR. If it also adds or changes a test, run that test
  (section 4) and check it the way section 5 describes. Also check that the mutant the write-up says
  it kills shows as killed in the `-after` report. Search the report for that location rather than
  reading it whole, since the reports can be large.
- **The PR is the user's own.** Nobody approves their own PR in this course. Say so, and offer a
  list of findings instead of a rubric.
- **This is a follow-up after the user asked for changes.** Check only the items they asked for.
  If those are done, suggest a short approval such as "All good now!"
- **The PR changes code or tests.** Do the full review described below.

## 3. Gather, lightly

Read these in order, and stop once you can score every rubric row:

1. The PR description, including its `## Test Evidence` section, and the linked issue's
   acceptance criteria (ACs) and design decisions. The rubric is scored against the ACs.
2. The diff. Skip `ai-logs/**`: those files are thousands of lines of chat transcript, and they
   are not reviewed.
3. The review bots' comments and the author's replies, so you don't repeat what was already raised
   and fixed:
   - **CodeRabbit**, configured by the repo's `.coderabbit.yaml`.
   - **Gitar** (Sonar's AI reviewer, mentioned as `@gitar-bot`), if the team turns it on. It keeps
     one dashboard comment that it updates on every push, holding its verdict and, when CI fails, a
     root-cause analysis. It also posts inline findings rated Critical, Important or Minor, and moves
     resolved ones into a collapsed section. Its rules, if any, are in the repo's `.gitar/` folder.
4. The CI status, if you can see it. Gitar's root-cause note on a failure is a lead, not a verdict;
   check it. If the course connects the repo to SonarQube Cloud, its quality gate shows up among the
   PR's checks.
5. SonarQube for IDE, if it's running in the user's VS Code and Claude Code is connected (`/ide`).
   Read its diagnostics for the PR's changed files. Only findings on changed lines count, and each is
   a lead to check like any other finding. If nothing shows, skip this step rather than setting it up.
6. Just enough of the code the diff touches or depends on to check its claims. In the clone,
   `.claude-students/INDEX.md` lists short docs for each area if you need background.

Don't run lint; CI does that. Do run the PR's tests (section 4), so the user doesn't have to. Don't
split the review across subagents.

Aim for about 10–15 tool calls for reading and checking, plus what the test runs need. In testing,
runs that went to 35 calls produced no better drafts than shorter ones would have. Spend those calls
on checking the findings that will go in the draft, one check each. Don't chase ideas you won't
include. Don't read the author's AI logs, and only download a library's source when a finding depends
on it. If you go over the budget, write the draft with what you have, and say what you didn't check.
Reviewers are expected to answer within 24 hours, which is one more reason to keep it short.

## 4. Run the PR's tests

In the clone, run the tests the PR adds or changes, plus the existing test files for the source files
it changes, and record the real counts. In chat you can't run anything: say so, give the user the exact
commands to run, and leave the testing line as a TODO.

- **Work in a throwaway worktree**, so the user's branch and their own server aren't touched:
  `git worktree add --detach .specstory/review-<N> pr-<N>`, then `CI=true pnpm install
  --frozen-lockfile` inside it. Never symlink `node_modules` into a worktree.
- **Unit tests:** `pnpm exec vitest run <files>` for the frontend, and `go test -run '<names>' ./<pkg>/`
  for Go. Go must match `go.mod`: a newer system Go breaks things, so put `~/sdk/go1.26.4/bin` first on
  `PATH` (check `go version` against `go.mod`).
- **Can the new unit tests fail?** This check is cheap. Restore the PR's changed source files to
  `origin/main` in the worktree, re-run the new unit tests, then restore the PR's versions. Tests for
  new behaviour should now fail. One that still passes may not test the change. Use it as evidence for
  the Test coverage row, not as a finding on its own.
- **Playwright tests the PR adds or changes:** `make test-e2e` can't run on this machine.
  1. Build the worktree (`make frontend backend`).
  2. Start its own server from a copy of `custom/conf/app.ini` with `WORK_PATH` set to the worktree
     and port 3001. Start it inside a helper script and stop it by PID, never with `pkill -f`. Create
     the `e2e-admin` user (password `password`) with `./gitea admin user create` if that instance
     doesn't have it.
  3. Run Playwright with a scratch config that extends `playwright.config.ts` and points Chromium at
     `/usr/bin/chromium` (`launchOptions.executablePath`). Set `GITEA_TEST_E2E_URL`,
     `GITEA_TEST_E2E_USER=e2e-admin`, `GITEA_TEST_E2E_PASSWORD=password` and
     `GITEA_TEST_E2E_DOMAIN=localhost`. Run on Chromium and Firefox.

  If the setup still fails after one fix, stop and say so; CI's e2e run is the fallback. The shell is
  zsh, so write environment variables out instead of using unquoted `$VARS`.
- **Read only the summary lines** of each run (pass, fail and skip counts, plus the names of any
  failures), not the full output.
- **A failure isn't a finding yet.** `multiselect-aria.test.ts` already fails locally on untouched
  main, and CI passes it. For any other failure, re-run it on `origin/main`. Only a failure the PR
  causes is a required fix, because the course allows no new test failures.
- **Clean up:** stop the server, then `git worktree remove --force .specstory/review-<N>`.

On a follow-up after new commits, re-run only the tests those commits touch.

## 5. What to check

- **Each AC.** Find where it is implemented and where it is tested. A missing AC is the main
  reason to lower the Correctness score.
- **Whether the tests can fail.** A test that would still pass with the feature removed doesn't
  count as coverage. Look for:
  - assertions that read a value without first asserting it exists;
  - `test.fail()` or skips that cover more than the one known failure;
  - checks that only test whether something is present.
- **The Test Evidence section** (required in every PR since Sprint 3). It needs:
  - one row per AC (for a bug fix, its Expected Behavior; for a PR with no behaviour change, "N/A"
    and a reason);
  - for each row, a named test or "Manual:" steps with what was seen;
  - a Level of unit, integration, E2E or manual;
  - a Source of expected value of AC, issue discussion, docs, upstream behavior, or other
    (explained);
  - a "Not tested automatically, and why" line that lists only the manual ACs;
  - an "AI-written tests" line, saying which tests and how their expected values were checked.

  Spot-check one or two rows: open the test, read its expected value, and compare it with the cited
  source. A value that only matches what the code happens to output (a pasted snapshot, or a number
  the AC never mentions) is exactly what the sprint page rules out.
- **Course rules that graders look at:**
  - `Closes #<N>` in the description, and the PR on the `Sprint 3` milestone;
  - a `## Tech Debt` section;
  - an AI assistance section;
  - before/after screenshots when templates, CSS or Vue files change;
  - Conventional Commit messages that end in `(#N)`;
  - `Assisted-by` trailers, and no `Co-Authored-By`;
  - commits small enough to review, for example split by layer;
  - a skipped test, `test.fail()`, `t.Skip` or disabled CI check has a linked issue and a reason in
    a code comment;
  - no new test failures: a red CI check on code the PR touches is a required fix;
  - commits pushed by a bot (for example a Gitar fix) are AI-made changes, so the AI section should
    mention them.

  A bot's approval (Gitar can auto-approve) doesn't count: the course needs a teammate's approval.

  The current sprint's rules are on https://csci-435-se.github.io/sprint3/. The repo's
  `.claude-students/COURSE-WORKFLOW.md` still described Sprint 2 on Nov 4, so where the two
  disagree, the sprint page wins.
- **Claims in the PR description.** Descriptions are often drafted by AI. Check one or two
  concrete claims against the code, such as a timing, a count, or "every test does X".

Check every finding against the source before it goes in the draft. Reviews of AI-written code
tend to produce confident findings that turn out wrong. A wrong finding in a posted review costs
the user more than a missed nit. If checking disproves your idea, drop the finding or reword it.
For example, on #105 a suspected "silent pass" turned out to fail loudly, so the finding became
about the unhelpful error message instead.

Leave out style nits, anything lint or CI catches, CodeRabbit or Gitar findings the author already
fixed (credit those in one line), and anything that wouldn't change a score. A bot or Sonar finding
that's still open goes in the draft only if you checked it against the code yourself. A Sonar rule
that fights Gitea's conventions isn't a finding.

## 6. Scoring

Start every row at 10, and deduct points only for a concrete gap you can name. Past reviews show
how the user scores:

- A UI change without before/after screenshots: Documentation 8, Overall 9, "Yes, once the
  screenshots are added".
- One large commit instead of commits split by layer: AI transparency 7.
- A factual error in the description or the Tech Debt section: Documentation 8.
- Everything checks out: 10s, and Overall 10, "Yes".

A deduction needs a *required* point behind it, something you would ask the author to change before
merging. An observation you'd only file under "Strictly optional" (one AC covered by unit tests but not
end to end, a small AI-assisted commit the description doesn't mention) leaves the score at 10. The user
has scored a feature PR 10 on every row even though optional observations like these existed.

Overall is "Yes" unless something required is missing. Nits don't block a merge. Any score below
7 needs a note saying what would raise it, because the course rubric requires one.

The test-evidence row is new, so there are no posted examples of it yet. Score it like the other
rows. A missing Test Evidence section, an AC with no row, or an expected value with no real source is
a required fix and lowers the score. A source that is valid but could be stronger is optional and
leaves it at 10. The row also asks which tests the reviewer ran locally: answer it from the section 4
runs, with real counts. If nothing could be run, put a visible `TODO (you): which tests you ran
locally` there instead.

## 7. Draft format

Use the rows from the course rubric. Read `.github/code-review-rubric.md` from the repo, or from
raw GitHub, so the draft picks up any change to the rubric. The template below matches the rubric
as of Sprint 3: the sprint page adds the test-evidence row. On Nov 4 the repo's rubric file didn't
have that row yet, so keep it even if the file still lacks it.

Write in the user's voice:

- short, plain sentences;
- one sentence per table note;
- no rule citations in the table;
- `file:line` for code findings.

Skim one of the reviews in `references/posted-examples.md` before you draft. These are reviews
the user actually posted.

```markdown
### Code Review — @ab-wm

Ran the PR's tests locally with Claude Code: <each command or file, with its pass/fail/skip counts>. TODO (you): anything you clicked or checked by hand, or delete this.

| Criterion | Score (1–10) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correctness — implements issue requirements | | |
| Test coverage — tests present and meaningful | | |
| Test evidence — does every AC have a test? Are the expected values justified? Which tests did you run locally? | | <finding>. Ran <which tests> locally: <counts>. |
| Code quality — style, naming, no duplication | | |
| Documentation — comments and PR description clear | | |
| AI transparency — evidence of human verification if AI used | | |
| Overall — merge as-is? | | |

### Strictly optional for completeness
**<the point in a few words>.** <one or two sentences, with file:line>

### AI-Log
Review was drafted by AI, and then changed to better fit the review structure and my inspection of the files. Log available on #<linked issue>.
```

- **Required changes** go in the note of the row they affect, written as a request ("please add
  before/after screenshots, as they are required"). Overall then says "Yes, once X is added".
- **Optional points** go in their own section after the table. Keep at most one or two, and drop
  the section if there are none.
- **The testing line** states only the test runs that really happened in section 4, with their
  counts, and says Claude Code ran them. What the user clicked or checked by hand stays a visible
  `TODO` for them to write or delete. Never fill it with your own checks; a visible placeholder can't
  be posted by accident without being noticed.

## 8. Hand it back

- **In Claude Code**, write the draft to `.specstory/pr-<N>-review.md` (the folder is
  gitignored). If that file already exists, it may be the user's edited copy, so write the draft
  to `pr-<N>-review-2.md` (or the next free number) instead.
- **In chat**, give the draft as one fenced markdown block, so the table copies cleanly.

Then write a short summary in chat, about 10–15 lines:

- the verdict;
- each finding, marked required or optional;
- the test results, and what you didn't run or check (for example, "e2e setup failed, so I relied
  on CI"), so the user knows what is left for them;
- any idea you couldn't verify, offered as something the user could try in their own testing.
  Unverified ideas never go in the draft.

End there. Remind the user to file this session's AI log in `ai-logs/sprint3/ab-wm/`, as
`ai-logs/README.md` describes, since the AI-Log section points to it. If they approve, mention once
that any commit the author pushes afterwards needs a new approval before the merge.

# Main's CI is red on every push and skips most test suites, and backend PRs wait about 28 minutes for checks
scope: medium | Sprint 3

## Problem

`main`'s CI status means nothing, `main` skips most of the test suites, and backend PRs are slow for a reason we can fix.

### Main is red on every push, so real failures go unnoticed

- `release-nightly-snapcraft` has failed or been cancelled on all 99 of its runs since the fork (78 failed, 21 cancelled, 0 passed). The latest one, [run 43539275792](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/43539275792), stops with `fatal: empty string is not a valid pathspec`. `snap/part-gitea-pull.sh:33` reads the newest tag with `%(tag)`, which is empty for lightweight tags, and all our `v1.27.3-csci435-*` tags are lightweight. Even with annotated tags it would fail at publish, because the repo has no Snap Store credentials and the `gitea` snap name belongs to upstream.
- `release-nightly` has never finished: 98 runs were cancelled and 1 is queued ([example](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/43537000589)). Its jobs need upstream's private `namespace-profile-gitea-release-*` runners. The next push cancels each run, or GitHub drops it after 24 hours in the queue.
- `release-tag-version` matches `v1.*`, so it has run for every sprint tag, and all three runs were cancelled after sitting queued for those runners: s0 ([35251424595](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/35251424595)), s1 ([37872246874](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/37872246874)) and s2 ([40956082407](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/40956082407)). The s3 tag will do the same.
- The noise is hiding a real failure. `db-tests` failed on `main` after two docs-only merges ([43345969430](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/43345969430), [43296442804](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/43296442804)) with the flaky `repo-issue-edit.test.ts` test from #171. Nobody noticed, because every `main` commit was already red.

### Main never runs most of the test suites

Every integration job in `pull-db-tests.yml` has `if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'` (lines 20, 56, 91, 188, 236), and `pull-e2e-tests.yml` runs only on pull requests too. A push to `main` runs `test-unit` and `sonarqube` (Go unit tests and Vitest coverage) and nothing else. Since PRs don't have to be up to date with `main` before merging, two PRs that each pass can break `main` together, and no integration or e2e run would show it. The Sprint 2 tag `v1.27.3-csci435-s2` (`40e0aa79`) has no test runs at all, so D8's Suite health section has no CI baseline to quote.

### Backend PRs take about 28 minutes, mostly compiling and waiting

Full backend `db-tests` runs take 23.3 to 30.1 min, with a median of about 27.6 (e.g. [43524265133](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/43524265133)). Waiting for a runner isn't the cause: the median wait is 2 seconds. The time goes to three things:

- The build cache is stale. `cache-seeder` has run once ([40807939468](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/40807939468), Oct 29), because it only triggers when `go.sum`, `.golangci.yml` or the cache files change. Its `gobuild-<go.sum hash>` key can never be overwritten, so the cache is now 141 commits behind `main`. It also warms the `-race` build but not `-race -cover`. As a result, each `test-unit` pass spends about 3.6 minutes compiling before the first package result, and every other Go test job compiles more than it should too.
- The two unit-test passes run one after the other. `test-unit` runs the normal pass (9.6 to 12.1 min) and then the `gogit` pass (9.4 to 11.5 min).
- `sonarqube` waits on `test-unit`. It has `needs: test-unit` and runs the Vitest coverage itself, so it can't start until both unit passes are done.

## Goal

`main` is green unless one of our own suites failed, it runs the integration and e2e suites after every merge and on every sprint tag, and anyone can run them against any ref. Backend PRs get the same checks as now, every database included, in noticeably less time.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC1: Given a push to `main`, when CI runs, then `release-nightly` and `release-nightly-snapcraft` show as skipped (not failed, cancelled or queued). Given a pushed `v1.*` tag, `release-tag-version` shows as skipped. `release-tag-rc` only triggers on `v1*-rc*` tags, which the course never pushes, so its guard is checked in the diff. Every job in the four workflows has the skip condition, with a same-line comment citing #181 and saying the workflow only runs upstream.
- [ ] AC2: Given any merge to `main`, docs-only ones included, when CI runs, then sqlite, MySQL, MSSQL and Postgres migration plus integration tests, Go unit tests, Vitest and the Playwright e2e suite all run against the merged commit. A newer merge never cancels a run that has already started. If several merges land while a run is in progress, only the newest waiting run is kept: the suites then run against the newest merged commit, and the replaced run shows as cancelled, never failed.
- [ ] AC3: Given a team member opens Actions → `db-tests` or `e2e-tests` → Run workflow and enters a ref (e.g. `v1.27.3-csci435-s2`), or someone pushes a `v*-csci435-*` tag, when the run finishes, then the suites from AC2 have run against that ref. A tag run or manual run never replaces a `main` run and is never replaced by one.
- [ ] AC4: Given a push to `main`, when CI runs, then the Go build cache is saved again under a key tied to that commit and includes the `-race -cover` build. Given a backend PR branched from `main` after that save, with no Go changes under `modules/` or `models/` (changes there recompile most of the tree whatever the cache holds), when `test-unit`'s normal pass runs, then the first package result appears at most 1 minute after `make test-backend` starts (about 3.6 minutes now).
- [ ] AC5: Given a backend PR, when `db-tests` runs, then the normal and `gogit` unit-test passes run as two separate jobs at the same time. Both run `make test-check`, and only the normal pass uploads Go coverage.
- [ ] AC6: Given any `db-tests` run, when it runs, then Vitest coverage runs in its own job, at the same time as the Go unit tests. `sonarqube` scans both coverage reports, and a failing Vitest test still makes the `db-tests` run fail. `sonarqube` runs only on pull requests and pushes to `main`, and is skipped on tag pushes and manual runs, so an old ref never replaces `main`'s analysis in SonarQube Cloud.
- [ ] AC7: Given the first attempt of four backend PR runs after the fix (a backend PR is one where `files-changed` reports `backend == 'true'`; re-runs don't count), when they finish, then the median wall-clock time of `db-tests` (from the run being created to its last job finishing, runner queue time included) is at most 22 minutes (about 27.6 now), and every job that ran on a backend PR before this change still runs. No database, `-race` or `gogit` coverage is removed. Only runs where no job waited more than 1 minute for a runner count toward the four, so the median doesn't depend on whether a `main` run was using the org's 20 job slots at the time. A run that did wait is replaced by the next backend PR run and listed with its wait time.
- [ ] AC8: Given `pull-db-tests.yml`, `pull-e2e-tests.yml` and `pull-compliance.yml`, then every job with steps has a job-level `timeout-minutes` of at most 60, so a hung job stops there instead of at GitHub's 6-hour default. The `files-changed` jobs are exempt: they call a reusable workflow, where GitHub doesn't allow `timeout-minutes`, and its `detect` job already has a 3-minute timeout.

## Out of Scope

- Fixing the flaky `repo-issue-edit.test.ts` test. That's #171. This issue makes sure such a failure turns `main` red where people will see it.
- The Postgres-only failures in `TestMilestoneBurndown/RealLifecycle` ([38276920412](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/38276920412) and two other branches) and `TestRepoCalendar` ([42658314475](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/42658314475)). The burndown one was a same-second ordering bug, already fixed in f5c361f00c. The calendar one is a data race in `timeutil.MockSet`, tracked in #185.
- Making status checks required, and protecting tags with a ruleset. Both need repo-admin rights. I'll propose them to the TA once AC2 is green, with one combined check job as the required check, because a skipped job counts as passing.
- Writing each suite's pass/fail/skip counts to the job summary, speeding up `lint-backend` (11 to 12 min, runs alongside the tests), and making individual integration tests faster (#37).

## Open Questions

None open. The one question, whether a 20-minute median was the right target for AC7, was settled on 2026-11-13 by measuring existing runs, and AC7 now says 22 minutes.

- **Fresh cache against stale cache.** The two backend PR runs from Oct 29, within a day of the only `cache-seeder` run ([40897202041](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/40897202041), [40897180193](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/40897180193)), took 19.8 and 16.7 min. The 14 successful backend PR runs from Nov 11 to 13 have a median of 28.8 min.
- **Where a database job's time goes.** From the job logs, compiling (`make backend`, the migration test binary and the integration test binary) takes 3.9 to 6.8 min per job with the stale cache and 0.8 to 1.3 min with a fresh one. The tests themselves take 9.4 to 12.3 min either way. With no compile time at all, MySQL and MSSQL still need 16 to 17 min each: about 3 for setup, 1 for migrations and 12 for tests.
- **Projection.** Taking each of the 14 recent runs, replacing its compile time with the fresh-cache figure and splitting the unit passes gives a median of 19.8 min, with 5 of the 14 over 20 and 2 over 22. The slowest job is a database job every time (MySQL 7 runs, MSSQL 5, sqlite 1, Postgres shard 1 once); unit tests plus `sonarqube` finish at 15 to 17.5 min.
- **Why 22 and not 20.** A 20-minute median would pass or fail on runner luck: MySQL alone ranged from 16.5 to 27.2 min on the same cache. Reaching 20 reliably means splitting both MySQL and MSSQL, since they take turns being slowest, which adds two jobs per PR against the org's limit of 20.
- **Limits of the measurement.** Only two fresh-cache runs exist, they predate `-cover`, and the suite has grown from about 720 to 729 integration tests since.

## Evidence of Fix

Broken or missing CI check: links to runs before and after.
- **Before:** the runs linked under Problem, and the backend `db-tests` times (median about 27.6 min) with the compile time from [43524265133](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/actions/runs/43524265133).
- **After:**
  - the first push to `main` after the merge, with release workflows skipped (AC1), every suite run (AC2) and the cache saved (AC4);
  - a manual run against `v1.27.3-csci435-s2` (AC3);
  - four backend PR runs with their times, their median and each job's compile time (AC4 to AC7);
  - the diff showing a job-level `timeout-minutes` on every job in the three files (AC8).

Every After item needs the change on `main`, so the PR's Test Evidence lists them as manual, post-merge checks, and the results go in a comment on this issue. The s3 tag push (`release-tag-version` skipped, suites run) only happens at the D9 release, after this issue closes, so it gets a follow-up comment here and isn't part of the closing evidence.

## Design Decision

### Decision 1: stopping the upstream release workflows

**Decision:** Add `if: github.repository == 'go-gitea/gitea'` to each job in the four release workflows, the same guard upstream already uses in `cron-*.yml` and `giteabot.yml`.
**Alternatives Considered:**
- *Fix the release workflows to work on the fork* (annotated tags, our own runners and store accounts). The team doesn't publish binaries, images or snaps, so this would be work for nothing.
- *Delete the files, or turn them off with `gh workflow disable`.* Deleting conflicts with upstream syncs. Turning them off can't be reviewed, only shows in the settings page, and is the kind of quiet silencing the course counts as small at most.
**Rationale:** These workflows publish upstream's builds and can't run here. The guard is upstream's own pattern, it goes through review in the diff, and a code comment records why.
**Consequences:** Their runs still appear in the Actions tab, marked skipped. If the team ever publishes its own builds, the guard has to come off.

### Decision 2: cutting backend PR time

**Decision:** Refresh the build cache on every push to `main`, run the two unit-test passes as parallel jobs, and move Vitest coverage out of the `test-unit` → `sonarqube` chain. Every database job still runs on every backend PR.
**Alternatives Considered:**
- *Run MySQL, MSSQL and Postgres on a PR only when it touches `models/`, `modules/setting/` or `services/migrations/`.* Rejected because the Postgres-only failures in `TestMilestoneBurndown` (three branches) and `TestRepoCalendar` came from `services/issue` and `routers/`, outside those paths, so they would have reached `main` without any warning.
- *Drop `-race` or the `gogit` pass on PRs.* That would save the most time, but it removes checks without fixing anything, and the course counts that as silencing.
- *Only add more shards.* It uses more runners for the same work, so PRs would start waiting on each other because of the org's limit of 20 jobs at once.
**Rationale:** Most of the extra time goes to compiling and to jobs waiting on each other. Fixing that shortens the run and keeps every check. Moving Vitest saves almost no time by itself: across the 14 backend PR runs from Nov 11 to 13, the `frontend-coverage` step took about 6 seconds and the whole `sonarqube` job a median of 2.9 min. The time saving comes from the cache and from splitting the unit passes. Vitest moves so that a failing frontend test shows up in the first minutes of a run; today it runs inside `sonarqube`, which waits for both unit passes, about 25 minutes in.
**Consequences:** One more job per backend PR. Each unit-test job sets up its own service containers. The 22-minute target is limited by the slowest database job, which is MySQL or MSSQL in most runs.

### Decision 3: how the cache gets refreshed

**Decision:** `cache-seeder` runs on every push to `main`. It saves under `gobuild-<go.sum hash>-<commit sha>` and warms `-race -cover` as well as `-race`. Only PR jobs restore with a `restore-keys` fallback to the newest entry. The seeder never restores an older build cache and always builds clean, so an entry holds one commit's build and doesn't grow from save to save. Update the comment at `.github/actions/go-cache/action.yml:7-8` to give the new reason.
**Alternatives Considered:**
- *Keep the key based only on `go.sum`.* A saved key can't be overwritten, so the cache never updates until `go.sum` changes.
- *Let PR jobs save the cache.* A PR's cache is only visible to that PR and the PRs based on it, so other PRs can't use it, and several jobs writing at once would fight over the same key.
**Rationale:** Caches saved from `main` are visible to every PR, and one key per commit means the newest build is always available.
**Consequences:** Each entry is about 2.25 GB against the repo's 10 GB cache limit, so GitHub keeps about four and evicts the oldest. The `gomod` and `golint` caches share that limit, so eviction can drop them too and slow `lint-backend` and module downloads. One extra seeder run per merge. A clean seeder build takes about 30 min (the Oct 29 run did), which no PR waits on; when merges come in a burst the newer seeder run cancels the older one, so the cache can lag until the last one finishes. The 2.25 GB is today's size without the `-race -cover` build, which will add to it and isn't measured yet.

### Decision 4: running the suites on `main` and on demand

**Decision:** Let the existing `pull-db-tests.yml` and `pull-e2e-tests.yml` jobs run on `push` to `main`, on `v*-csci435-*` tags and on `workflow_dispatch` (with a `ref` input that checkout uses), by changing each `pull_request`-only condition to `github.event_name != 'pull_request' || <the existing files-changed check>`. Pushes to `main` share one concurrency group with `cancel-in-progress` false, so a running job is never cancelled. Each tag and each manual run gets its own group, so it neither waits on nor replaces a `main` run. Pull request runs keep the group they have now.
**Alternatives Considered:**
- *A new `main-suites.yml` that copies the jobs.* The copies would drift away from the PR jobs.
- *Turn the jobs into one `workflow_call` workflow used by both.* No copies, but it rewrites upstream's files the most, which makes upstream syncs harder.
- *Keep the `files-changed` filter on pushes to `main`, so docs-only merges skip the suites.* Most merges here are docs-only, and the two `db-tests` failures linked under Problem both came after docs-only merges, so repeat runs on an unchanged tree are how a flaky test shows up. Replacing the waiting run caps the cost at one queued run.
**Rationale:** Changing the conditions keeps one definition for each job and touches as few upstream lines as possible. Starting a run by hand with a `ref` input works for old tags, which don't have this workflow file.
**Consequences:** About 12 jobs per merge on `main` (10 in `db-tests`, 2 in `e2e-tests`), plus the two `cache-seeder` jobs. When merges come in bursts, a waiting run is replaced by the newest one, so a failure may cover more than one merge, and the replaced run shows as cancelled on its commit; that saves runner time against the org's limit of 20 jobs. Every suite still `needs: files-changed`, so on push, tag and manual runs that job has to succeed (or be bypassed) even when it has no base to compare against, or every suite is skipped. A manual run takes the workflow file from `main` but `.github/actions/*` and the Makefile from the ref it checks out. `v1.27.3-csci435-s2` has the same actions and make targets as `main`; a ref from before those existed may not run.

## Scope

medium, `scope: medium`. Changes `pull-db-tests.yml`, `pull-e2e-tests.yml`, `pull-compliance.yml` (timeouts), `cache-seeder.yml`, the `go-cache` action and the four release workflows. No product code changes. Evidence needs several pushes to `main`, a tag push, a manual run against a tag and four timed PR runs, each checked against the before numbers.

Closes #181

## What changed

This changes CI configuration only, with no product code.

- The four `release-*` workflows have `if: github.repository == 'go-gitea/gitea'` on every job, so on this fork they show as skipped.
- `db-tests` and `e2e-tests` also run on pushes to `main`, on `v*-csci435-*` tags and from Run workflow with a `ref` input, which every checkout uses. On those events every suite runs; pull requests still filter by `files-changed`.
- Concurrency: pull requests keep their per-branch group. Pushes to `main` share the group `<workflow>-refs/heads/main` with `cancel-in-progress` off, so a running suite is never cancelled and only the waiting run gets replaced. Tag and manual runs each get a group of their own.
- `files-changed.yml` skips detection on anything but a pull request, so the job always succeeds and every output is empty there.
- `cache-seeder` runs on every push to `main`. The gobuild key is now `gobuild-<os>-<arch>-<go.sum hash>-<sha>`, PR jobs fall back to the newest entry, and the seeder has no fallback, so it builds clean. It warms `-race -cover` for the normal tags.
- The `gogit` unit pass moved to a new job, `test-unit-gogit`. Both unit jobs run `make test-check`; only `test-unit` uploads Go coverage.
- Vitest coverage moved to `test-frontend-coverage`, which has no `needs`. `sonarqube` needs it and `test-unit`, downloads both reports, and runs only for same-repo pull requests and pushes to `main`.
- Every job with steps in `pull-db-tests.yml`, `pull-e2e-tests.yml` and `pull-compliance.yml` has a job-level `timeout-minutes` from 20 to 60. The two `cache-seeder` jobs got one too.
- Updated `sonar-project.properties`, `.claude-students/docs/build-and-tooling.md` and its guide twin.

## Why

`main` was red on every push because of release workflows that can't run here, it never ran the integration or e2e suites, and backend PRs took about 27.6 minutes, mostly compiling against a cache 141 commits old and running the two unit passes back to back. This covers AC1 to AC8 of #181. AC7's timing can only be measured once this is on `main` and the cache has been saved.

## CI / manual verification

Locally: `make lint-actions` (actionlint) reports no findings, `yamllint` on the changed YAML files is clean, and `./.claude-students/check.sh` passes. This PR touches no Go files, so its `db-tests` run only runs `test-sqlite` (it filters on `actions`), `test-frontend-coverage` and `sonarqube`; the unit and database jobs are skipped as before.

## Design

Follows the four Design Decisions in #181, with four changes:

- **Seeder build flags.** The seeder warms `-race -cover` for the normal tags in place of plain `-race`, because no job runs the normal tags without coverage any more. The `gogit` build still warms plain `-race`. Rejected: keeping plain `-race` only, which leaves `test-unit` compiling the coverage build from scratch and misses AC4; and warming both `-race` and `-race -cover` as the issue's wording allows, which makes each cache entry bigger for a build nothing restores.
- **Concurrency group for `main`.** The group is `<workflow>-refs/heads/main`. A fork PR from its own `main` branch has `head_ref` `main`, and with `cancel-in-progress` on, it would cancel our `main` run. Rejected: `<workflow>-main`, which has that collision; and prefixing the pull request group (`<workflow>-pr-<head_ref>`), which also avoids it but changes the PR group the issue says to keep.
- **`sonarqube` keeps installing frontend dependencies.** Only the Vitest run moved out, so the TypeScript analysis can read types from `node_modules` as it did before. Rejected: skipping the install, which saves about a minute but can change what the scan reports and isn't on the critical path; and passing `node_modules` from `test-frontend-coverage` as an artifact, which adds a large upload and download for no time saved.
- **Seeder runs are no longer cancelled.** Decision 3 let a newer seeder run cancel the older one, but a cancelled run saves nothing and a clean build takes about 30 minutes, so merges landing closer together than that would never refresh the cache. `cancel-in-progress` is now false: a running seeder finishes and saves, and a newer push only replaces the waiting run. Rejected: keeping the cancel, which can starve the cache during a burst of merges; and a per-commit group, which runs every queued seeder and adds a 30-minute job per merge against the org's 20-job limit.

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:** `test-unit-gogit` copies `test-unit`'s service containers, about 40 lines, so a change to one has to go into the other. A matrix would share them, but the two passes need different `GOEXPERIMENT` handling and only one uploads coverage. The `cache-seeder` `lint` job now runs on every merge too, though its golangci-lint cache key only changes with `go.sum` or `.golangci.yml`.

**Encountered:** The golangci-lint cache has the same key problem the gobuild cache had: it can't be overwritten until `go.sum` or `.golangci.yml` changes. Speeding up `lint-backend` is out of scope for #181, so I left it.

+- **`.github/workflows/cache-seeder.yml` saves the Go build cache on every push to `main`**, keyed
+  by `go.sum` and the commit SHA; pull request jobs restore the newest entry
+  (`.github/actions/go-cache/action.yml`). The normal and `gogit` unit-test passes are separate
